tier_reason: Upgraded from B to A. The peer-reviewed paper (Bioinformatics 39 Suppl. 1, i534) compares LPHash against BBHash and PTHash. It states the Intel i9-9900K CPU, gcc 11.2.0 and the flags -O3 -march=native. The benchmark code is public in the repo: src/ptbb/ptbb_build.cpp and src/ptbb/ptbb_query.cpp build and query BBHash (external/BooPHF.hpp) and PTHash, and scripts/experiments.sh runs them.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper Table 3: partitioned LPHash at k=63 uses 0.53, 0.64, 0.83, 0.58 and 0.87 bits/k-mer on Yeast, Elegans, Cod, Kestrel and Human. BBHash-v1 uses 3.71 bits/k-mer, BBHash-v2 3.06, PTHash-v1 2.58-2.76 and PTHash-v2 2.04-2.20. The paper states LPHash is 5.1x, 4.1x, 3.2x, 4.4x and 3x smaller than PTHash-v1 and 2.3-3.7x smaller than PTHash-v2. Against BBHash-v2 it is about 3.5-5.8x smaller (derived from page data). At k=31, LPHash uses 1.18-1.74 bits/k-mer. For streaming queries the paper says: 'Compared to BBHash, LPHash is 2x faster on Yeast and up to 4-5x faster on the larger datasets.' The README's claim of '< 0.9 bits/k-mer vs 1.44 lower bound and 2-3 bits/k-mer for practical constructions' matches these tables.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 11.2.0, -O3 -march=native (paper). The repo CMakeLists.txt also adds -std=c++17 -mbmi2 -msse4.2.
corrections.hardware: Intel i9-9900K @ 3.60 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Linux 5.13.0. Queries ran on 1 core. Builds used 4 threads.
corrections.workload: An MPHF over the distinct k-mers of 5 whole-genome datasets, from Yeast (11.6M k-mers) to Human (2.77G k-mers), given as spectrum-preserving string sets (BCALM2 + UST stitched unitigs), for k=31..63. Space is measured in bits/k-mer. Queries are about 100M k-mers from human chr13, measured in streaming and random order on a single core.
corrections.caveats: The space win applies only to overlapping k-mers from spectrum-preserving string sets. The paper stresses that BBHash and PTHash are general-purpose MPHFs for arbitrary keys. Random-order (non-streaming) queries are slower than PTHash. Construction is slower than BBHash-v1: Table 5 gives 05:30 vs 00:48 on Cod and 07:25 vs 04:13 on Human. Datasets are on Zenodo (record 7239205). The last commit on the default branch (main) is 2023-07-19. The dev branch has a later commit, dated 2023-11-18.

notes: The paper names BBHash and PTHash as the competitors, so the 'unnamed baseline' caveat and the 0.4 confidence cap no longer apply. maintenance_status follows the prescribed commits?per_page=1 method (main, 2023-07-19, more than 3 years ago = abandoned). If the dev-branch commit (2023-11-18) is used instead, the status is 'stale'. The orchestrator may prefer that date.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C to A. The peer-reviewed ALENEX'23 paper compares SicHash against BBHash and cmph (CHD, BDZ, BMZ, FCH). It states the Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3 CPU, GCC 11.1.0 and the flags -O3 -march=native. The benchmark code is public: the paper and README point to github.com/ByteHamster/SicHash (src/sicHashBenchmark.cpp, Dockerfile) and to github.com/ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments (contenders/fingerprinting/BBHashContender.cpp, contenders/bucketplacement/ChdContender.cpp).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper (ALENEX 2023): SicHash 'dominates the Pareto front for load factors from 0.85 to 0.97' in construction throughput vs space for N=5M and N=20M. The competitors are BBHash, cmph's CHD, BDZ, BMZ and FCH, PTHash, RecSplit and WBPM. The paper says: 'For some space requirements, SicHash can be constructed up to 3 times faster than the next best competitor.' Appendix Table 1 (N/M=0.95): SicHash uses 1.75 bits/object at 3.27 MObjects/s. PTHash uses 1.76 at 0.61 and RecSplit 1.78 at 0.76, so SicHash builds about 4.3-5.4x faster at the same space (derived from page data). Against BBHash the comparison is only in plots. BBHash is configured at 3.5-4.0 bits/object, against 1.8 for the PHFs (Figure 5). In the Figure 5 query plot, SicHash has higher query throughput than BBHash at every N from 10^6 to 2x10^8.
corrections.workload: Construction throughput vs bits/object Pareto fronts for N = 1M, 5M and 20M keys at load factors 0.8-0.97 and for minimal perfect hashing. Query throughput is measured for N = 10^6 to 2x10^8. Keys are random strings of length 10-50. All runs are single-threaded. The competitors are BBHash, cmph (CHD, BDZ, BMZ, FCH), PTHash, RecSplit and WBPM.
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3 @ 2.3 GHz, Ubuntu 20.04, Linux 5.10.0. The appendix also shows an AMD Ryzen 3950X and an ARM Neoverse-N1.
corrections.caveats: Numbers against BBHash and cmph appear only as plots. The paper's only numeric table (Appendix C) compares SicHash with PTHash and RecSplit. In the construction plots, BBHash reaches the highest raw construction throughput, but at much larger space (3.5-4.0 bits/object). SicHash wins on space at comparable build throughput and on query throughput. The competitor benchmarks are in a separate repo (ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments, GPL-3.0), which has changed since the 2022 paper. The license is GPL-3.0 (copyleft).

notes: The record's 'metric: memory' does not fit well. The paper's claim is construction throughput at a given space, plus query throughput, so 'throughput' fits better, but metric is not a correctable field. The claimed_speedup in the record had no numbers, so numbers_found_on_page is null. It has been replaced with figures stated in the paper.

tier_reason: Not Tier A, because the repo is PRIVATE (gh api reports visibility 'private'), so the benchmark code is not public. The search agent's claim that bench/bench_phf.cpp 'is public' is wrong. results/fastest.json (run 2026-09-02-core, commit dfa74f2) states the numbers, gcc 13.3.0, the flags and the CPU. bench/bench_phf.cpp does benchmark std::unordered_map<string_view,uint16_t>. The numbers are first-party and not peer-reviewed, so the tier is C.

corrections.caveats: The repo is PRIVATE and readable only with an authenticated gh CLI, so the benchmark code is not public and the entry cannot be Tier A. List readers will get a 404 on repo_url and benchmark_url. It has 0 stars. It is a single-author project: all 13 commits are authored by 'Claude' with Claude co-author trailers, and nobody outside has reviewed it. The CPU is given only as 'Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz' (shared cloud VM, no SKU). The results file warns that absolute ns vary between runs (3.42 vs 5.24 ns for the same lookup) and that only ratios within one run are meaningful. The std::unordered_map numbers come from commit dfa74f2 at -O2 -std=c++20. HEAD CMake now forces -O3 and C++23 for benchmarks, so a rerun at HEAD would not use the recorded flags. The frozen::unordered_map figure (3.55x in results/fastest.json, '3.5-3.7x' in the notes) cannot be reproduced. bench/bench_vs_libraries.cpp, at HEAD and at 2e21aae, benchmarks only fastcpp::phf, phmap::flat_hash_map and std::unordered_map, and mentions frozen only in comments. The repo has no gperf comparison: gperf does not appear in the README or in results/fastest.json. The PHF techniques are reimplemented from strager's talk; the README says no code was copied from strager/perfect-hash-tables (CC-BY-NC-ND).

notes: All three std::unordered_map numbers match results/fastest.json exactly. bench/bench_phf.cpp at commit dfa74f2 is identical to HEAD. The phmap 3.7x figure is 19.787/5.322 ns (3.72x). The orchestrator should decide whether a private repo can go in COPYABLE at all. It has an MIT license, but the public cannot get the code.
